newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU lawyers study British govt's Social Chapter move.
newsitem.headline: EU lawyers study British govt's Social Chapter move.

text.p: An announcement by Britain's new Labour government that it is ready to sign the European Union's Social Chapter has sent lawyers scurrying to find out exactly how it should be done.

The government said on Sunday it would take the first steps toward adopting the text, officially known as the Social Protocol, at a meeting on Monday of the inter-governmental conference (IGC) which is preparing a new EU treaty.
But questions remain about whether it must wait for a new treaty to be signed and ratified by all 15 EU national parliaments or whether it can take the protocol's provisions on board more quickly.
Spokeswomen for the British government and the European Commission said lawyers were studying the question.

"We are in the process of consulting the Legal Service of the Commission at the moment to see how this will be dealt with formally and if there's any way of accelerating the process," Commission spokeswoman Barbara Nolan told a news briefing.

The Social Protocol, attached as an annex to the Maastricht Treaty signed by EU countries in 1992, allows EU governments to bypass Britain and adopt labour laws in areas ranging from worker consultation to social security.
The Commission has asked the IGC to integrate the protocol into the treaty proper, but had no chance of succeeding while Britain's Conservatives were in power.
Former prime minister John Major, defeated in last week's election, argued that laws adopted under the text would overburden industry and kill jobs.

The EU has adopted two laws under the Social Protocol so far -- the "works council" directive requiring big multinational companies to set up procedures for consulting their workers and the "parental leave" directive guaranteeing three months of unpaid leave to new parents, both male or female.
Nolan said nothing should prevent Britain from turning those directives into national law, whether or not it has officially signed on to the Social Protocol.
The works council directive is already in force, but governments have until June 3, 1998 to implement the parental leave directive.
Another question for the lawyers is whether Britain can take part immediately in negotiations on other legislation which has been proposed under the Social Protocol.

EU ministers are now debating a draft law, for example, which would require employers to share the burden of proof with plaintiffs in sex discrimination suits, with final agreement expected in the second half of the year.
"These are the sort of technical issues we have to look at," Nolan said.
